name: Zane Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work new claims for housing benefit at the Northgate benefits office, second floor, the bank of desks by the broken radiator. I'm in at half eight, log into the case system, and work the queue: rent statements, payslips, tenancy agreements, people's whole lives in scanned PDFs. Ruth, my team leader, still checks about a third of my decisions because I'm only two years in and I still get the earnings rules wrong sometimes. The best bit is the phone calls where you can actually fix something for someone before their landlord sends a notice.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The backlog, mostly. We're meant to clear a claim in fourteen days and we're at about twenty-five, so every call starts with someone angry, and fair enough. And the system itself, which crashes after lunch most days. I go home to Dani, my partner, who drives the number 9 bus, and we compare who got shouted at more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that's the one I'd bet on. Every year someone from head office shows us a new tool that's going to change everything, and six months later we're still printing things out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say told you so, mostly to Kofi, our union rep, who's been saying the same. Online I'd probably share something about how the money should have gone on hiring staff instead. We're short six caseworkers on my floor and no chatbot fixes that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, but not fully. Even a small tool that pre-fills the income section would be aimed at work like mine, the routine checking that juniors do. The senior people do the judgement calls, and I'm not there yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly I'd keep doing what I do, and try to get better at the earnings rules so Ruth stops checking a third of my work. I'd keep paying the union subs, that's twelve a month and worth it. And I'd keep putting about two hundred a month into savings, because the rent on our flat goes up every spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, but not comfortable. The rent and the backlog were already there before any of this AI talk. Picturing nothing changing is a relief, but it's also picturing the same broken radiator for ten more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a small tool would be aimed at work like yours. What part of your day would it touch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The data entry. Typing the rent figure off a tenancy agreement and matching the landlord's bank details. If a tool does the boring typing, my managers will say a junior caseworker only needs half a day, and they'll count the hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would worry you first if your hours did get cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rent, it's nearly half of what I bring home. Dani's shifts are steady, but we split everything down the middle, so I couldn't just lean on that. I've got about three months saved, which sounds fine until you picture the spring rent letter.

say: I'd tell colleagues the AI hype was **all talk** and the real fix is more staff.
I'd post that the money should have gone on **hiring caseworkers** instead of tools.
think: I'm relieved, but even small tools target the **routine checking** juniors like me do.
My **hours** could be counted more tightly if a tool does the typing.
do: Keep learning the **earnings rules** so my team leader checks less of my work.
Keep paying **union subs** and putting about **two hundred** a month into savings.
feel: **Steady but uncomfortable**, because the rent and backlog were problems before any AI talk.
S0.quote: If a tool does the boring typing, my managers will say a junior caseworker only needs half a day, and they'll count the hours.
fieldNote: His first worry is the **rent rise** each spring, not AI at all.
He links even small automation to managers **counting hours** of junior staff.
Union membership is part of how he feels **protected** at work.

steps.text: Study the earnings rules until Ruth checks fewer of his decisions
Put about two hundred a month into savings before the spring rent rise
Keep paying union subs and talking with Kofi about staffing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one makes my stomach drop a bit, because checking and answering customers is literally my job description. Writing letters too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it at the union branch meeting first: no tool decides someone's housing without a human signing it off. Online I'd be louder, probably arguing with people who say the public sector is bloated. I'd say these are people's homes, not parcels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think they'd stop hiring juniors first, and I'm the junior. The senior caseworkers would be kept to sign things off, and people like me would be offered a transfer to the phone line. And the phone line would be the next thing the AI takes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting and put my name down for the staffing working group. I'd stop the weekend trips to see my cousins and push savings up to three hundred a month. And I'd look at what other public jobs nearby need people, the council's housing team or the job centre, and ask Ruth for a reference while she still likes me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit stubborn about it. I don't want to learn to babysit a machine that takes my work. But I know being stubborn doesn't pay the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never use these tools. If your office brought one in, would you refuse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd use it if they made me, I just wouldn't trust it. I'd double-check everything by hand, which would make me slower, which would make me look worse. I'd be the guy checking the robot's homework while the robot gets the credit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, who sits next to me, she's newer than me and on a temporary contract. If they cut, it's temporary contracts first. I'd worry about her before me, and then about me.

say: I'd say **no tool** should decide someone's housing without a human signing off.
I'd argue online that benefits are **people's homes**, not parcels to process faster.
think: I expect them to **stop hiring juniors** first, and I'm the junior.
A transfer to the **phone line** would only delay it, because AI takes that next.
do: Join the union's **staffing working group** and attend every branch meeting.
Raise savings to **three hundred** a month by dropping weekend trips.
Ask my team leader for a **reference** and look at council housing jobs.
feel: **Anxious** and stubborn, not wanting to babysit a machine that takes his work.
S1.quote: I'd be the guy checking the robot's homework while the robot gets the credit.
fieldNote: He would use AI if ordered but **distrusts** it so much he'd slow himself down.
He thinks of **temporary staff** like Priya before himself, which fits his union outlook.
He expects junior posts to **vanish quietly** through no new hiring rather than layoffs.

steps.text: Join the union branch's staffing working group this winter
Drop weekend trips to his cousins and save three hundred a month
Ask Ruth for a reference and apply to the council housing team

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before I'd even finish my probation on the next grade. I don't think the office would know what to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has to stop it or slow it, full stop. I'd be on the march, if there's a march. Public services shouldn't be handed to a company that can switch them off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think my job's gone by 2028. Everything I do is on a screen: read the documents, check the numbers, write the decision letter. Even the phone calls. The only part a machine can't do yet is sit with someone at the counter, and by 2031 the robots come for that too, if anyone even wants a counter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd stop spending on anything but rent and food, and get the savings from three months to as close to six as I could. I'd push the union to fight for redeployment, not redundancy, for every caseworker. And I'd ask Dani's depot about training as a bus driver, because driving is hands-on and that gives me maybe three more years, which is better than nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the floor's moving. I'm twenty-seven and I'd be starting again with a two-year diploma that suddenly means nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've been against using AI. Would two years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd change whether I can afford to be against it. I'd still be against it, I'd just have no time to make a point about it. My whole skill is reading a payslip carefully, and a machine that reads a million payslips a second makes that skill worth nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Dani that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we need to sit down with the bank statements, both of us, not just me worrying alone. That if both our jobs go, his three years after mine, we should plan as one household. And probably that we shouldn't sign the new two-year lease.

say: I'd say the government must **slow it down** and keep public services human.
I'd join any **march** against handing benefits to a company that can switch them off.
think: I believe my job is **gone by 2028**, because nearly all of it is screen work.
The counter work lasts only until **robots arrive** around 2031, if counters even survive.
do: Cut spending to **rent and food** and push savings towards six months.
Press the union to fight for **redeployment**, not redundancy, for every caseworker.
Ask the bus depot about **driver training** for a few extra years of hands-on work.
feel: **Alarmed**, as if the floor is moving under him.
Afraid his **diploma** would suddenly count for nothing at twenty-seven.
S2.quote: My whole skill is reading a payslip carefully, and a machine that reads a million payslips a second makes that skill worth nothing.
fieldNote: He sees his work as almost **all thinking work**, so the stated date hits him directly.
He uses the **three-year robot gap** practically, aiming for bus driving as a bridge.
His resistance to AI becomes something he **can't afford**, not something he drops.

steps.text: Cut spending to rent and food and aim for six months saved
Push the union to demand redeployment for every caseworker
Ask Dani's bus depot about driver training places
Hold off signing the new two-year flat lease

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is still fast, but it's not a cliff. At least you'd see it coming down the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to write rules, so let's use them. A law that says a person signs every benefit decision. I'd sign every petition going and I'd vote for whoever promised that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In private I think five years only means I'd watch it happen slowly. The juniors would go first, then the phone team. I'd have time to plan, but I'm not the kind of person who plans well for things I don't want to happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give myself one year to get onto the next grade, because seniors get kept longer. In that year I'd save hard, maybe four hundred a month if we moved somewhere cheaper. And I'd campaign with the union for a guaranteed retraining fund for public staff, paid before the cuts, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed, just more slowly. It's like being told the building will be demolished in five years while you're still decorating your desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you move, if you moved somewhere cheaper?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Out past the ring road, near Dani's depot, where a two-bed is cheaper than our one-bed now. Longer bus for me, shorter for him. We've talked about it before, this would just make us do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't plan well for things you don't want. What would make you start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Somebody I trust saying it out loud, like Ruth or Kofi. If my team leader Ruth sat me down and said the junior posts are going in 2030, I'd finally stop pretending.

say: I'd say we have **five years** to write rules and should use them.
I'd back a **law** that a person signs every benefit decision.
think: I'd watch the **juniors go first**, then the phone team, slowly.
I admit I **avoid planning** for things I don't want to happen.
do: Try for the **next grade** within a year, since seniors are kept longer.
Move past the ring road to save about **four hundred** a month.
Campaign for a **retraining fund** for public staff, paid before cuts.
feel: Still **alarmed**, like decorating a desk in a building set for **demolition**.
S3.quote: If my team leader Ruth sat me down and said the junior posts are going in 2030, I'd finally stop pretending.
fieldNote: Five years doesn't calm him, because his **job loss** still looks likely.
He openly admits he **avoids planning** and needs a trusted person to push him.
He looks to **law and the union** before his own career change.

steps.text: Apply for the next caseworker grade within a year
Move with Dani to a cheaper two-bed past the ring road
Sign petitions and vote for a human sign-off law
Campaign with the union for a public staff retraining fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a whole career-change window, if I actually took it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the same end, so the fight is the same: who owns it and who gets the savings. If AI saves the government billions on staff, put it into housing. I'd say that at work and at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years makes me lazy about it. I'd probably keep my head down for five of them. But I know my job is the kind that goes first, so I'd be kidding myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and get the senior grade, then start an evening course around year three, probably in social work or housing support, something with home visits. I'd keep saving the two hundred a month. And I'd stay in the union, because ten years of warning is ten years of bargaining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but breathing. There's room to turn around. I just don't trust myself to turn without being pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why social work or housing support rather than something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's going into people's homes, seeing the damp, sitting with someone. A computer can read a tenancy agreement, but somebody still has to knock on the door and see the mould on the bedroom wall. Robots by 2039, sure, but I'd want a person knocking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change anything with Dani?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe we'd finally think about kids, around thirty. With two years I'd say no way. With ten I'd want to, but I'd want one of us in a job that's still there.

say: I'd say the real question is **who gets the savings** from cutting staff.
I'd argue the money saved should go into **housing**, at work and at the pub.
think: Ten years could make me **lazy**, keeping my head down for half of it.
I know my job is the **kind that goes first**, so waiting is self-deception.
do: Reach the **senior grade**, then start an **evening course** around year three.
Keep saving **two hundred** a month and stay active in the **union**.
feel: **Anxious but breathing**, with room to turn around if pushed.
S4.quote: A computer can read a tenancy agreement, but somebody still has to knock on the door and see the mould on the bedroom wall.
fieldNote: More time eases his panic but not his expectation of **losing the job**.
He moves towards **home-visit work** because it is partly hands-on and personal.
Family plans like **children** depend on how much warning he gets.

steps.text: Start an evening course in housing support around year three
Keep saving two hundred a month in the joint account
Stay active in the union to bargain over the decade

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. It's not that it's the worst ending, it's that there's no time to do anything except panic quietly. What would help is a promise in writing that public staff get retrained on full pay before anyone's let go, and a rent freeze, honestly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who decides. Everyone asks what I'd do, but I'm a junior on a housing desk, I don't decide anything. I can save two hundred a month and go to union meetings, but someone in a tower decides if the Northgate benefits office still exists.

headlineQuote: I can save two hundred a month and go to union meetings, but someone in a tower decides if the Northgate benefits office still exists.
portrait: Zane is a **27-year-old** junior housing benefit caseworker who lives with his partner Dani, a bus driver.
He is a loyal **union member**, never uses AI, and distrusts tools that count junior hours.
He moves from **uneasy** about rent in AI Plateau to **alarmed** in both faster AGI pictures.
He looks to **law, the union** and partly hands-on work like home visits for protection.
He admits he **avoids planning** for change he dislikes and needs a trusted push.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there'd be no time to do anything but quietly panic.
whatWouldHelp: A written promise of **retraining on full pay** before any public staff are let go.
A **rent freeze** to ease the pressure on his household.
